messages.author: fbff4100433066b4
messages.subject: parallelization
parts:
So other than letting STAN detect the number of cores to run chains in parallel, is there anything we can do make STAN programs run faster?

I am working on a Windows PC 3.7 GHz processor, 32 GB RAM, and 4 cores.

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parallelization
parts:
Yup, when you sample, just set the cores argument:

post = rstan::sampling(
    object = my_stan_model
    , data = my_data_for_stan
    , cores = parallel::detectCores() #if you want to use all your cores, else put a number
)


--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parallelization
parts:
Each iteration of an MCMC chain is dependent on the last iteration. This means that each *chain* cannot be parallelized (not sure what will happen if/when Stan implements multiple crawlers to find multimodality for each chain though).

This is unlike other monte carlo techniques, like bootstrapping, because each iteration is functionally independent on any other iteration. Markov chains are defined to have dependent sampling, so each iteration is dependent on the previous iteration to some degree.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parallelization
parts:
Two things.

1. In my experience, setting it to the number of physical
cores rather than "hyperthreaded" cores results in faster
code.

2. While we can't literally parallelize chains because of
the Markov dependency, we can parallelize all the code to
compute the density and derivatives. Often in big models that's
a big matrix operation or solutions to ODEs with random effects
so you need to run the solver a number of times proportional
to the data. In general, if the density can be broken into
chunks where the partial derivatives can be computed, they can
be packed back together into an expression graph for which you
can do autodiff. The autodiff itself, which is over 90% of
a Stan's program execution, can also be parallelized.

We're thinking about how to do all these things. Stay tuned.
Most likely thing we'll get going next is Eigen matrix operations
with GPU (CUDA) and multithreading (OpenMP) support. Sebastian
Weber's already done the latter successfully and it resulted
in the natural massive speedup---it's nearly embarassingly parallel
when most of the compute time is in the parallelizable operation.

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parallelization
parts:
The short answer is yes. The Eigen library has parallelization. 

It's tricky to configure. I've been meaning to write a blog post about how I set up my machine to make OpenMP work. Rob Trangucci and I were able to figure it out.

Once configured, it's simple getting it working with CmdStan. 

But beware: in most situations, single core will be faster. (You didn't misread that: using the wrong number of cores or if the size of the problem isn't the right scale, I saw run times of 2-5x.) On the problem we were looking at, after a lot of experimentation, we got it to run faster by something like 15%. That was on a laptop, so with a large machine, I could see there being larger gains. 


Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parallelization
parts:
I'm pretty sure Sebastian set up OpenMP to solve ODEs
in parallel rather than to just turn on OpenMP for
Eigen.

What we want to figure out how to do is turn on GPUs for
Eigen. Should be easier now that they added support in 3.3
and we're now running with 3.3.

- Bob

> On Nov 18, 2016, at 5:40 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> The short answer is yes. The Eigen library has parallelization.
>
> It's tricky to configure. I've been meaning to write a blog post about how I set up my machine to make OpenMP work. Rob Trangucci and I were able to figure it out.
>
> Once configured, it's simple getting it working with CmdStan.
>
> But beware: in most situations, single core will be faster. (You didn't misread that: using the wrong number of cores or if the size of the problem isn't the right scale, I saw run times of 2-5x.) On the problem we were looking at, after a lot of experimentation, we got it to run faster by something like 15%. That was on a laptop, so with a large machine, I could see there being larger gains.
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
> On Nov 18, 2016, at 5:26 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Is this available in any github branches yet? I'd love to give it a spin.
>>
>> On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 11:26:12 AM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Two things.
>>
>> 1. In my experience, setting it to the number of physical
>> cores rather than "hyperthreaded" cores results in faster
>> code.
>>
>> 2. While we can't literally parallelize chains because of
>> the Markov dependency, we can parallelize all the code to
>> compute the density and derivatives. Often in big models that's
>> a big matrix operation or solutions to ODEs with random effects
>> so you need to run the solver a number of times proportional
>> to the data. In general, if the density can be broken into
>> chunks where the partial derivatives can be computed, they can
>> be packed back together into an expression graph for which you
>> can do autodiff. The autodiff itself, which is over 90% of
>> a Stan's program execution, can also be parallelized.
>>
>> We're thinking about how to do all these things. Stay tuned.
>> Most likely thing we'll get going next is Eigen matrix operations
>> with GPU (CUDA) and multithreading (OpenMP) support. Sebastian
>> Weber's already done the latter successfully and it resulted
>> in the natural massive speedup---it's nearly embarassingly parallel
>> when most of the compute time is in the parallelizable operation.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>> > On Nov 18, 2016, at 11:48 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >
>> > Each iteration of an MCMC chain is dependent on the last iteration. This means that each *chain* cannot be parallelized (not sure what will happen if/when Stan implements multiple crawlers to find multimodality for each chain though).
>> >
>> > This is unlike other monte carlo techniques, like bootstrapping, because each iteration is functionally independent on any other iteration. Markov chains are defined to have dependent sampling, so each iteration is dependent on the previous iteration to some degree.
>> >
>> > On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 9:25:09 AM UTC-6, Vishv Jeet wrote:
>> >
>> > You mean if I have access to a 64 cores machine I can massively parallelize STAN code even if I am using 4 chains?
>> >
>> >
>> > On Friday, November 18, 2016 at 10:12:47 AM UTC-5, Mike Lawrence wrote:
>> > By the way, I suspect that while that machine has 4 physical cores, it can do 8 things in parallel thanks to hyperthreading. I'm not sure if parallel::detectCores() will return 4 or 8, but you could try 4, see if your cpu usage is maxed (use task manager), and if not bump it up to 8.
>> >
>> >
>> > --
>> > Mike Lawrence
>> > Graduate Student
>> > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
>> > Dalhousie University
>> >
>> > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
>> >
>> > On Fri, Nov 18, 2016 at 11:10 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > Yup, when you sample, just set the cores argument:
>> >
>> > post = rstan::sampling(
>> > object = my_stan_model
>> > , data = my_data_for_stan
>> > , cores = parallel::detectCores() #if you want to use all your cores, else put a number
>> > )
>> >
>> >
>> > --
>> > Mike Lawrence
>> > Graduate Student
>> > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
>> > Dalhousie University
>> >
>> > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
>> >
>> > On Fri, Nov 18, 2016 at 10:52 AM, Vishv Jeet <vishv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >
>> > So other than letting STAN detect the number of cores to run chains in parallel, is there anything we can do make STAN programs run faster?
>> >
>> > I am working on a Windows PC 3.7 GHz processor, 32 GB RAM, and 4 cores.
>> >
